<reason>Both sides were disciplined, but PRO controlled the decisive definitional and comparative ground. CON's central strategy — collapsing PRO's camera/ticket enforcement into "penalties" — was clever and forced PRO to clarify, but it quietly substitutes "any consequence" for the motion's actual rival lever, "harsher post-crash penalties." PRO held that line cleanly (certainty vs severity; pre-crash small fine vs post-death sentencing) and then converted CON's honest Q1 answer ("Yes — I'd fund the camera-and-20mph program") into a direct concession on the motion as written. CON's best independent route was coverage and incapacitation: redesign protects specific pavement while revocation/jail removes dangerous drivers everywhere. PRO neutralized this twice: first that geometry constrains the driver deterrence has already provably failed on, then decisively that a *default* limit is a single citywide vote that reaches the very 90% of unrebuilt grid CON relied on — reframing CON's "slow and local" charge as false. PRO also raised, and CON never answered, the identification burden: incapacitation requires a prior crash to find the dangerous driver, so the first-time impaired or distracted driver (the ordinary fatal case) sits entirely outside CON's mechanism. CON's Oslo/Houston pushback (paper penalties, sprawl, vehicle mass) was its sharpest counterpunch, but it conceded PRO's marginal-leverage framing rather than defeating it. CON's closing largely restated the equivocation frame instead of resolving the default-limit and identification pressures, while PRO's closing crystallized the choice memorably.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's closing turn on CON's own frame: against "redesign protects specific pavement, block by block," PRO pointed out the motion's first half is a *default* speed limit — one vote, citywide overnight, covering exactly the unrebuilt 90% CON leaned on — paired with the unanswered point that incapacitation must first identify the dangerous driver, and does so only via a crash.</best_rebuttal>
